references.text: Jesus already predicted early in his ministry that he must suffer greatly, be rejected and killed, and rise on the third day – it is to these words he refers back in [ref:Luk 9:22|Luke 9:22].

Jesus told the disciples that everything written by the prophets about the Son of Man must be fulfilled – he would be handed over, mocked, mistreated, spat upon, flogged and killed, but rise again on the third day ([ref:Luk 18:31-33|Luke 18:31-33]).

Earlier that same day, Jesus explained to the travelers on the road to Emmaus that the Messiah had to suffer these things and enter into his glory, and he began with Moses and all the prophets and interpreted for them what was written about him in all the Scriptures ([ref:Luk 24:26-27|Luke 24:26-27]).

Jesus says that he has not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets, but to fulfill them ([ref:Matt 5:17|Matthew 5:17]). This aligns with the fact that everything written about him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.

Jesus asks how then could the Scriptures be fulfilled, which say that it must happen this way ([ref:Matt 26:54|Matthew 26:54]). This underscores the necessity that the words of Scripture about him are fulfilled.

Peter proclaims that what God foretold through all his prophets, namely that his Messiah would suffer, he has now fulfilled ([ref:Apg 3:18|Acts 3:18]). This is a direct fulfillment of what Jesus spoke about.

Paul testifies that he says nothing other than what the prophets and Moses said should happen: that the Messiah must suffer, and that as the first to rise from the dead, he would proclaim light to the people and to the Gentiles ([ref:Apg 26:22-23|Acts 26:22-23]).

Paul in Rome explained these things to them and testified about the kingdom of God, trying to persuade them concerning Jesus from the Law of Moses and the Prophets ([ref:Apg 28:23|Acts 28:23]), which reflects Jesus' division of Scripture.

[ref:Sal 22:1-31|Psalm 22] is a messianic psalm that describes the cry of the suffering righteous one and details that were fulfilled in Jesus' suffering – this is part of what Jesus refers to with "the Psalms".
[ref:Sal 110:1-4|Psalm 110:1-4] is the most quoted psalm in the New Testament and speaks of the Messiah sitting at God's right hand – a central part of "what is written in the Psalms" about Christ.

[ref:Jes 53:1-12|Isaiah 53:1-12] is the prophecy about the Lord's suffering servant who bears our sicknesses and sins. This is the core of what the prophets have written about the Messiah, which Jesus refers to.
Moses prophesied that the Lord God would raise up a prophet like him from among his people ([ref:5 Mos 18:15|Deuteronomy 18:15]). This is part of "the Law of Moses" that points forward to Christ.

Jesus immediately expands that the Messiah must suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations ([ref:Luk 24:46-47|Luke 24:46-47]).

Paul writes that the gospel concerning God's Son was promised beforehand through the prophets in the holy Scriptures ([ref:Rom 1:2|Romans 1:2]), confirming Jesus' words that the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms testify about him.

Peter writes that the prophets carefully searched and investigated the salvation that was foretold, trying to find out what time or situation the Spirit of Christ in them pointed to when it testified beforehand about Christ's sufferings and the glory that would follow ([ref:1 Pet 1:10-11|1 Peter 1:10-11]).
